title: A Catholic doubter
hookLine: he remained Catholic and died during Mass in 1592, while doubting nearly everything else

cards: A pair of scales, two pans hanging level. Montaigne took that image as his emblem, he says, with a short question beside it: what do I know? The same man submitted his writing to the judgment of the Church he was born in.
He put the doubt and the faith in the same book, and hid neither one. Readers still argue about him, and about what that question left room for.

teach.h: OUR SENSES AND REASON FOOL US.
teach.b: First, the doubt. In the Apology for Raymond Sebond, Montaigne takes apart human confidence piece by piece. Our senses fool us.
Our reason argues both sides of anything. Animals may know things we don't. Even the skeptics' own claim, I doubt, says too much, he thinks, because it sounds sure of itself.
So he turns it into a question: what do I know? Second, the faith.
In the essay Of prayers, he says he puts his thoughts forward as things to be explored, not truths to be believed, and submits them to the Church he was born in.
He'd gladly see Christians use the Lord's Prayer at every turn. Third, how he holds them together, and here readers differ.
Some read a sincere Catholic who thinks reason is too weak to reach God, so faith must come as a gift, not a proof. Some read the faith as a careful cover for a deeper doubt.
Some say we simply can't see inside him, which would suit him well. Fourth, the end.
Tradition says Montaigne died while Mass was being said in his room: the doubter, at the end, inside the rite of his church.
Whatever you make of him, he didn't think faith and doubt had to evict each other. A scale doesn't need one pan empty to hang level.

how: Readers of Montaigne differ on how to hold his doubt and his Catholic faith together: some read him as a sincere believer who thought reason could not reach God, others read the faith as a cover, and some leave the question open.

o: a skeptic who mocked prayer in all of his essays
Montaigne: asking what do I know?, yet staying in his Church

games.q: you're Montaigne. even the skeptic's I doubt sounds too sure of itself. how do you put your doubt into words?
o: as a question: what do I know?
games.why: he turned it into a question and set it beside an image of balanced scales.

practice: Let your hands rest open, one on each knee, like the two pans of a scale. In one, place something you trust, whatever that is for you: a person, a practice, a belief, the sun coming up; in the other, a question you can't answer.
Don't let either hand win; just feel the weight of both.

wordCard.voice: A Catholic doubter. Montaigne, who asked what do I know?, stayed in the Church he was born in, and tradition says he died during Mass. Today's word.

orig.note: Montaigne's French, in the Latin alphabet: what do I know? his question in the Apology for Raymond Sebond, beside the image of a balance.

carryVoice: Your line: faith and doubt. He let them share a room, and neither one had to leave. Until tomorrow.
